text:
Understanding the Global Lithium Supply Chain Architecture

The lithium mining sector represents one of the most strategically significant extractive industries in the modern economy, with global production networks spanning continents and technologies. Understanding these operations requires examining the complex interplay between geological endowments, technological capabilities, and market positioning that determines long-term competitive advantages.

Market Fundamentals and Production Metrics

Global lithium production reached approximately 1.4 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) in 2024, representing a substantial 22% increase from the previous year according to U.S. Geological Survey data. This expansion reflects the sector's response to accelerating demand from battery manufacturers and energy storage applications.

Production capacity measurement distinguishes between theoretical maximum output and actual realized production, which faces constraints from ore grade variations, processing efficiency limitations, operational maintenance requirements, and cyclical market demand. Current global nameplate capacity exceeds actual output by approximately 18-25%, indicating significant underutilization during market downturns.

Key Performance Indicators for Mining Operations:

• Reserve-to-production ratios measuring operational longevity

• Processing yield rates reflecting technological efficiency

• Unit cost metrics measured in USD per tonne LCE

• Geographic distribution across major producing regions

• Capital efficiency metrics for large-scale operations

The geographic distribution reveals three primary production clusters: South America accounts for 55% of global production through predominantly brine operations, Australia contributes 35% via hard rock spodumene extraction, and China provides 8% using mixed methodologies. However, reserve distribution differs significantly from current production patterns, with South America holding approximately 62% of global reserves, Australia 18%, and China 8%.

Investment Grade Classification Systems

Lithium operations are increasingly categorised using sophisticated classification frameworks that evaluate multiple operational and strategic dimensions. Tier 1 operations typically demonstrate annual production exceeding 50,000 tonnes LCE, while Tier 2 operations range between 20,000-50,000 tonnes annually, and Tier 3 operations produce less than 20,000 tonnes.

Reserve Quality Assessment Framework:

Classification Production Threshold Reserve Base Strategic Value Tier 1 >50,000 tonnes LCE >30 year horizon Global supply impact Tier 2 20,000-50,000 tonnes 15-30 year horizon Regional significance Tier 3 <20,000 tonnes <15 year horizon Niche market focus

Capital efficiency metrics have become increasingly sophisticated, incorporating not only traditional return on invested capital measures but also environmental compliance costs, technological advancement requirements, and geopolitical risk adjustments. Operations with downstream processing capabilities command 15-25% production price premiums compared to concentrate-only producers.

What Drives Lithium Mine Rankings in 2025?

Contemporary lithium mine evaluation frameworks have evolved beyond simple production volume assessments to incorporate multidimensional strategic value metrics. These frameworks recognise that sustainable competitive advantage in lithium mining derives from the intersection of geological endowments, technological capabilities, and strategic positioning within global supply chains.

Production Volume Analysis Framework

Lithium carbonate equivalent standardisation enables direct comparison across diverse production methodologies. One tonne of lithium metal equals approximately 5.32 tonnes of lithium carbonate or 8.56 tonnes of lithium hydroxide, providing the foundation for consistent performance measurement across brine and hard rock operations.

Processing capacity calculations incorporate multiple efficiency factors including ore grade, extraction technology performance, and downstream processing throughput. Hard rock operations typically achieve 85-92% lithium recovery rates, while brine operations demonstrate more variable performance ranging from 50-85% depending on evaporation cycle effectiveness and brine chemistry.

The global reserve-to-production ratio currently approximates 93 years at existing extraction rates, significantly exceeding fossil fuel extraction horizons that average 40-50 years. This extended timeframe indicates lithium supply sustainability relative to projected demand growth, though individual operation sustainability varies considerably based on specific geological characteristics.

Technology Impact on Production Efficiency:

• Direct lithium extraction technologies increasing hard rock efficiency by 15-30%

• Advanced brine concentration methods reducing evaporation timelines

• Automated processing systems improving yield consistency

• Environmental remediation technologies reducing regulatory compliance costs

Major producers currently operate at 70-85% nameplate capacity as of Q2 2025, reflecting cyclical market conditions and contracted customer demand patterns. This utilisation rate indicates potential for rapid production increases when market conditions warrant capacity expansion.

Strategic Value Assessment Criteria

Supply chain integration capabilities represent fundamental strategic moats in lithium mining operations. Companies controlling extraction through refining and chemical processing create customer lock-in effects and demonstrate superior margin resilience during market volatility periods.

Geopolitical stability analysis encompasses political risk evaluation, regulatory predictability assessment, treaty compliance history, and dispute resolution effectiveness. Regions with established democratic institutions and rule of law frameworks demonstrate measurably lower operational disruption risk profiles.

Environmental Compliance Impact Analysis:

Operation Type Water Consumption Carbon Intensity Regulatory Complexity Brine Operations 65-400 m³/tonne Li 5-8 tonnes CO2-eq/tonne LCE High (water rights) Hard Rock Mining 15-50 m³/tonne Li 8-12 tonnes CO2-eq/tonne LCE Medium (tailings)

Environmental compliance in lithium mining directly impacts operational sustainability through water consumption requirements, carbon intensity considerations, and tailings management obligations. Water-intensive brine operations in arid regions face increasing regulatory scrutiny, while hard rock operations encounter tailings containment and acid mine drainage concerns.

Regional Market Dynamics and Competitive Landscape

Regional specialisation in lithium extraction reflects geological endowments, technological capabilities, and infrastructure development patterns that have evolved over decades of mining operations. These regional advantages create sustainable competitive positioning that influences global supply chain architecture.

South American Brine Operations Dominance

South American lithium production totaled approximately 561,000 tonnes LCE in 2024, representing roughly 40% of global production. Argentina contributed approximately 145,000 tonnes, Chile produced 380,000 tonnes, and Bolivia added 36,000 tonnes with emerging capacity development. Furthermore, the Argentine lithium market insights reveal significant expansion potential across major brine operations.

The Lithium Triangle spanning Argentina, Chile, and Bolivia contains approximately 385 million tonnes of lithium reserves, representing 62% of the global total. This concentration creates both supply security and geopolitical risk considerations for downstream battery manufacturers.

Salar-Based Extraction Economic Advantages:

• Production costs of $3,000-$4,500 per tonne LCE

• Natural brine concentrations reducing initial processing requirements

• Solar evaporation minimising energy consumption

• High-altitude salar locations providing optimal evaporation conditions

Brine extraction leverages natural lithium concentrations in salt flats at elevations of 3,500-4,500 meters, reducing extraction depth requirements and initial capital investments. The Atacama region's salar deposits contain lithium brines with concentrations of 600-1,200 mg/L, substantially higher than most global alternatives.

Climate dependency creates inherent supply-side volatility in South American operations. Drought conditions reduce evaporation-based extraction cycles, while heavy precipitation disrupts brine concentration processes. This structural volatility differentiates salar operations from hard rock mining alternatives.

The brine extraction process requires 12-24 months for solar evaporation to concentrate lithium from initial concentrations of 0.3-0.8% to refined lithium carbonate at 95-99% purity. This extended timeline minimises processing costs but maximises land and water requirements, creating environmental and community conflicts in water-scarce Andean regions.

Hard Rock Mining Operations: Australian Leadership

Australian lithium production reached approximately 500,000 tonnes LCE in 2024, representing 36% of global production through predominantly spodumene-based hard rock mining. Australia dominates global spodumene concentrate production with approximately 65% market share, particularly through Australian lithium industry innovations that enhance operational efficiency.

Australian hard rock operations benefit from geological advantages including large, high-grade deposits with lithium concentrations in spodumene ore of 5-8% lithium oxide. Established mining infrastructure, regulatory certainty, and developed downstream processing ecosystems create sustainable competitive advantages.

Spodumene Processing Technology Framework:

• Conventional underground and open-pit extraction methods

• Ore crushing to 10-30mm particle size specifications

• Flotation separation producing 5-6% Li2O concentrate

• Thermal roasting at 900-1,100°C for chemical activation

• Downstream conversion to battery-grade lithium compounds

Modern spodumene processing achieves lithium extraction rates of 85-92%, representing a 12-15% improvement over processing methods deployed prior to 2015. These technological advances directly impact production economics and competitive positioning.

Export logistics present both challenges and opportunities for Australian producers. Shipping costs of $200-400 per tonne for delivery to Asian processing facilities, with European delivery adding $350-500 per tonne, influence strategic partnership development and downstream integration decisions.

Australian producers increasingly develop coordinated relationships with Asian battery material manufacturers, creating supply chain advantages through integrated transportation and chemical conversion processes. This vertical integration reduces total supply chain costs by 8-12% compared to spot market transactions.

Market Leaders: Production Excellence and Strategic Positioning

Contemporary lithium mining evaluation employs sophisticated analytical frameworks that extend beyond traditional production volume metrics to encompass strategic value creation, operational resilience, and long-term sustainability factors.

What Makes a Tier 1 Lithium Operation?

Comprehensive Assessment Matrix:

Evaluation Criteria Weighting Measurement Methodology Industry Benchmarks Annual Production Volume 40% LCE tonnes verified output >50,000 tonnes (Tier 1) Reserve Base Quality 25% Geological assessment & longevity >30 year operational horizon Cost Efficiency Leadership 20% USD per tonne total cost analysis Bottom quartile industry costs Strategic Market Value 15% Supply chain integration & partnerships Downstream processing capabilities

Tier 1 operations demonstrate sustained production excellence through consistent operational performance, technological innovation deployment, and strategic market positioning that influences global lithium supply chains. These operations typically maintain production costs in the bottom quartile of industry benchmarks while demonstrating superior operational reliability.

Critical Success Factors for Market Leadership

Market-leading lithium operations exhibit common characteristics that differentiate them from mid-tier competitors. These include geological advantages providing long-term resource security, technological capabilities enabling superior extraction efficiency, and strategic positioning within global battery supply chains. However, emerging projects like the Thacker Pass lithium mine demonstrate how strategic locations can create new market leaders.

Operational Excellence Indicators:

• Production consistency exceeding 95% nameplate capacity utilisation

• Unit cost performance in bottom 25% of industry benchmarks

• Reserve replacement exceeding annual production through exploration

• Environmental compliance maintaining regulatory approval status

• Customer contract portfolios spanning multiple end-market applications

Financial performance metrics for leading operations typically demonstrate superior return on invested capital, margin stability during commodity price volatility, and successful capital allocation for expansion projects. These financial characteristics reflect operational efficiency and strategic market positioning advantages.

Technology deployment distinguishes market leaders through advanced processing methods, automation implementation, and environmental performance optimisation. Leading operations invest 3-5% of annual revenue in research and development activities focused on efficiency improvements and environmental impact reduction.

Investment Implications and Market Outlook

Contemporary lithium mining investment analysis requires sophisticated evaluation of multiple risk and return factors that extend beyond traditional commodity investment frameworks. The sector's strategic importance to global energy transition creates unique investment dynamics combining traditional mining fundamentals with technology sector growth characteristics.

Capital Allocation Trends Across Producer Tiers

Investment priorities vary significantly across operational tiers, reflecting different strategic objectives and market positioning requirements. Tier 1 producers focus on capacity expansion and technological advancement, while emerging producers prioritise market entry and operational optimisation.

Investment Priority Framework by Operational Tier:

Operational Tier Primary Investment Focus Capital Intensity Expected ROI Timeline Tier 1 Leaders Capacity expansion & technology High ($500M-2B) 3-5 years Tier 2 Operations Processing optimisation & efficiency Medium ($100M-500M) 2-4 years Emerging Producers Market entry & infrastructure Variable ($50M-300M) 5-7 years

Tier 1 operations demonstrate superior capital allocation efficiency through integrated expansion strategies that simultaneously increase production capacity and improve operational efficiency. These investments typically generate returns exceeding 15-20% internal rate of return under base case demand scenarios.

Supply Chain Risk Assessment Framework

Geopolitical concentration represents a fundamental risk factor in lithium supply chains, with South America accounting for 60% of current production. Sustained disruption in this region would create significant global supply chain vulnerability requiring strategic diversification initiatives.

Multi-Dimensional Risk Analysis:

• Geographic concentration risk across producing regions

• Political stability factors and regulatory environment volatility

• Environmental compliance requirements and operational constraints

• Technology disruption potential and adaptation capabilities

• Market demand volatility and cyclical pricing patterns

Environmental compliance requirements increasingly influence operational sustainability through water consumption regulations, carbon intensity targets, and community impact considerations. Operations in water-stressed regions face particular scrutiny regarding aquifer depletion and agricultural water competition.

Technology disruption potential encompasses both opportunity and risk dimensions. Geothermal lithium extraction technologies offer processing efficiency improvements while potentially reducing environmental impact, but require substantial capital investment and operational expertise development.

Future Market Evolution and Strategic Considerations

The lithium mining sector approaches a critical inflection point characterised by accelerating demand growth, technological innovation deployment, and evolving regulatory frameworks that will reshape competitive dynamics over the next decade.

Emerging Technologies and Production Methodologies

Direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology represents the most significant technological advancement in lithium production since the development of modern brine evaporation methods. DLE technologies potentially reduce production timelines from 12-24 months to 30-90 days while improving extraction efficiency.

Technology Innovation Impact Areas:

• Processing timeline reduction through advanced extraction methods

• Water consumption minimisation via recycling and efficiency improvements

• Energy intensity reduction through renewable power integration

• Waste stream optimisation reducing environmental impact

• Automation deployment improving operational consistency

Recycling integration creates circular economy opportunities as lithium-ion battery waste streams mature. Battery recycling could contribute 10-15% of global lithium supply by 2030, potentially reducing primary extraction requirements and creating new competitive dynamics.

Alternative brine processing innovations focus on reducing evaporation dependence through membrane separation, selective precipitation, and electrochemical extraction methods. These technologies address climate dependency concerns while potentially improving extraction efficiency.

Hard rock mining efficiency improvements concentrate on ore sorting technologies, flotation process optimisation, and integrated processing facility design that reduce unit costs and environmental impact simultaneously. Moreover, advanced battery-grade lithium refinery facilities are increasingly important for meeting growing demand.

Market Demand Projections and Capacity Planning

Electric vehicle adoption rate impacts create the primary demand driver for lithium markets, with global EV sales projected to reach 30-40 million units annually by 2030. Each vehicle requires approximately 8-15 kg of lithium depending on battery chemistry and pack size.

Demand Growth Scenario Analysis:

Application Sector 2024 Demand 2030 Projection Growth Rate Electric Vehicles 850,000 tonnes LCE 2,200,000 tonnes LCE 14.5% CAGR Energy Storage Systems 180,000 tonnes LCE 550,000 tonnes LCE 17.2% CAGR Consumer Electronics 120,000 tonnes LCE 160,000 tonnes LCE 4.9% CAGR

Energy storage system growth requirements represent the fastest-growing demand segment, driven by renewable energy integration and grid stabilisation requirements. Utility-scale battery storage installations could require 550,000 tonnes LCE annually by 2030.

Supply-demand balance scenarios through 2030 suggest potential supply constraints developing if project development timelines extend beyond current expectations. New lithium operations typically require 5-8 years from discovery to production, creating supply response delays relative to demand acceleration.

Strategic reserve considerations reflect government recognition of lithium's critical mineral status. Several jurisdictions implement strategic stockpiling programmes and domestic production incentives to reduce import dependency and supply chain vulnerability.

Frequently Asked Questions About Global Lithium Mining

Understanding lithium mining evaluation requires familiarity with industry-specific terminology, assessment methodologies, and market dynamics that differ substantially from conventional commodity mining sectors.

How Are Lithium Mine Rankings Determined?

Lithium mine rankings employ multidimensional evaluation frameworks that incorporate production volume, reserve quality, operational efficiency, and strategic market positioning. Production volume methodology measures verified annual output in lithium carbonate equivalent terms, enabling direct comparison across different extraction methods.

Ranking Methodology Components:

• Annual production verification through independent audits and company reporting

• Reserve quality assessment incorporating geological surveys and proven reserves

• Operational efficiency analysis including cost structure and capacity utilisation

• Strategic market value evaluation considering supply chain integration and customer relationships

Data verification processes rely on company financial reports, geological survey publications, industry analysis platforms, and regulatory filing requirements. Third-party verification ensures ranking accuracy and consistency across global operations.

Reserve quality assessment evaluates not only total lithium content but also extraction complexity, processing requirements, and long-term operational viability. High-grade deposits with favourable geology command premium valuations despite potentially smaller absolute reserve sizes.

What Factors Drive Lithium Production Costs?

Production cost structures vary dramatically between extraction methodologies, with brine operations demonstrating lower unit costs but higher capital intensity, while hard rock mining requires higher operating costs but offers production timeline advantages.

Cost Structure Analysis by Extraction Method:

Cost Component Brine Operations Hard Rock Mining Direct Extraction $800-1,200/tonne $1,500-2,200/tonne Processing & Refining $1,200-1,800/tonne $2,000-2,800/tonne Infrastructure & Logistics $400-800/tonne $600-1,200/tonne Environmental Compliance $300-600/tonne $500-900/tonne Total Production Cost $3,000-4,500/tonne $5,000-7,500/tonne

Geographic location influences production costs through labour availability, energy costs, transportation requirements, and regulatory compliance expenses. Operations in remote locations face higher logistics costs but may benefit from lower labour and land acquisition expenses.

Processing technology advancement directly impacts unit costs through improved extraction efficiency, reduced energy consumption, and enhanced automation deployment. Leading operations achieve 8-12% cost advantages through technological superiority.

Regulatory compliance costs encompass environmental monitoring, water management, community relations, and government royalty payments. These costs typically represent 10-15% of total production expenses and continue increasing in most jurisdictions.

Which Regions Dominate Global Lithium Production?

Regional production dominance reflects geological endowments, technological capabilities, and infrastructure development that create sustainable competitive advantages for specific extraction methodologies.

South American salar operations leverage exceptional geological conditions including high-altitude salt flats with concentrated lithium brines, favourable evaporation climates, and substantial reserve bases. The Lithium Triangle countries collectively control 62% of global lithium reserves.

Regional Production Characteristics:

• South America: Brine-based extraction, low unit costs, climate-dependent production

• Australia: Hard rock spodumene mining, technological leadership, export orientation

• China: Mixed extraction methods, downstream processing dominance, domestic market focus

• Emerging Regions: North America, Africa development projects with strategic government support

Australian spodumene mining maintains leadership through geological advantages, established infrastructure, regulatory stability, and technological innovation. Western Australia contains high-grade spodumene deposits with favourable extraction characteristics.

Geopolitical considerations increasingly influence production location strategies as governments recognise lithium's strategic importance. Supply security concerns drive domestic production incentives and international partnership development.

Emerging production regions including North America and Africa develop projects focused on supply chain diversification and regional market supply. These projects typically emphasise technological advancement and environmental performance optimisation.

Happy Halifax Resolves Day, celebrating the moment when, on April 12, 1776, North Carolina declared months before the Declaration of Independence that it wanted its independence from Great Britain, which of course included paying taxes to the crown.

More on the Halifax Resolves in a moment.

Let’s talk more about taxes.

Democratic Gov. Josh Stein and Republican leaders are generally at odds over tax cuts. Simply put, Senate Republicans want to keep planned individual income tax cuts, House Republicans want to slow those cuts unless there’s enough revenue, and Stein wants tax cuts to just freeze.

Stein told his fellow elected officials on the Council of State that “painful cuts” may be ahead if the General Assembly doesn’t adjust the levels of state revenue that trigger tax cuts. These triggers have been at the center of the budget stalemate.

“Things are going very well in the state, but if we don’t have a fiscally responsible budget, we’re all going to have to make exceedingly painful cuts to the work that we do as a state,” Stein said.

Stein was in the Senate in 2009 when lawmakers had to cut 20-25% of the state budget, Stein said.

“It was awful,” he said. “We either had to cut it or raise taxes to do that.”

Stein told The News & Observer he plans to make another budget proposal to lawmakers as they come back to Raleigh for the short session that begins April 21.

Beyond income tax rates, both Stein and state lawmakers are looking at other policy that impacts revenue: tax exemptions.

Stein questioned the tax breaks data centers receive, saying that, “If all planned data centers in North Carolina are built, developers would receive an estimated $450 million in sales tax exemptions each and every year. And with the state’s impending fiscal cliff and the federal government retreating on longstanding commitments, state revenue is especially precious.”

He went on to say that “we should spend taxpayer dollars only when it adds value to our people. And do we really want to subsidize energy consumption by data centers when they are making everyone else’s power bills go up? It doesn’t make much sense to me.”

Beyond scrutinizing sales tax exemptions, lawmakers are taking a very close look at property tax exemptions. The House Select Committee on Property Tax Reduction and Reform will meet again this week — on Tax Day. Representatives have been considering whether to reduce some exemptions, including for affordable housing and hospitals.

Lawmakers on that committee plan to vote on moving proposed legislation ahead that would let voters decide if there should be a cap on property tax rates, which are set by local governments. Over on the Senate side, leader Phil Berger appointed some senators to look at the issue, but there is no committee or action yet.

Stein will be at Halifax ceremony, inducted into Sons of American Revolution

Stein will be inducted into the Raleigh chapter of the Sons of the American Revolution today in Halifax. A member of the local chapter made the announcement during a legislative committee meeting this week about celebrating America’s 250th birthday.

The Council of State’s monthly meeting was held at the visitor center at the historic Halifax site, and statewide elected officials had a chance to see the actual, original 1776 Halifax Resolves up close. I wrote about why it’s here and what else is being planned to celebrate America250 this year in North Carolina, including a Fourth of July Parade in Raleigh.

Sunday, when Stein returns to Halifax, is the last of three Halifax Resolves Days, which includes living history demonstrations, music, tours and the resolves on display.

North Carolina’s Halifax Resolves will be back home for America250 celebration

‘Huge celebration’ in NC for Fourth of July with Raleigh parade, America250 events

And for our new Under the Dome podcast episode posting Tuesday, you can hear more about the Halifax Resolves, passed on the date commemorated on our state flag and state seal.

Thanks for reading. Reach me at dvaughan@newsobserver.com or the entire politics team at dome@newsobserver.com.

title: The Real EV Problem May No Longer Be the Cars, but Where You Charge Them
description:
JD Power says public charging is still the top stumbling block to broader EV adoption, even as concerns about purchase price have started to ease.
The Durham, North Carolina-based network, led by CEO Seth Cutler, says it wants to build at least 30,000 fast charging bays across North America by 2030.

Charging Is Still the Real Bottleneck For all the progress in battery technology, charging confidence remains the weak link.
JD Power reported that 16% of public charging station visitors in the first quarter of 2025 still failed to charge, even after a notable improvement from late 2024.
text:
As automakers keep improving EV range and pushing prices lower, the biggest remaining obstacle is starting to look less like the drivetrain itself and more like the charging experience around it. JD Power says public charging is still the top stumbling block to broader EV adoption, even as concerns about purchase price have started to ease.

That is where Ionna enters the picture. The Durham, North Carolina-based network, led by CEO Seth Cutler, says it wants to build at least 30,000 fast charging bays across North America by 2030.

Its pitch is not just about adding more plugs. It is about building stations that work reliably and feel like places drivers would actually choose to stop.

And unlike a year ago, Ionna is no longer just selling a plan. In March 2026, the company said it had already passed 100 live sites and nearly 1,000 live charging bays nationwide.

Charging Is Still the Real Bottleneck

For all the progress in battery technology, charging confidence remains the weak link. JD Power reported that 16% of public charging station visitors in the first quarter of 2025 still failed to charge, even after a notable improvement from late 2024.

That helps explain why Ionna keeps talking more about dependability than sheer scale. In a March 2026 interview, Cutler said the company was seeing 99.5% uptime across its first 97 live sites, with systems in place to detect problems quickly and dispatch technicians fast.

That approach matters because public perception has not caught up with recent improvements. JD Power found that many shoppers still treat charging availability and charging confidence as major reasons to reject EVs, which means a network that simply works could carry as much weight as another jump in vehicle range.

Ionna Wants Charging To Feel Normal

Reliability is only part of the problem. Many public charging locations still feel like an afterthought, tucked into poorly lit or inconvenient corners that make the stop itself feel like a penalty instead of a routine part of travel.

One early example of Ionna’s answer sits in West Point, Georgia, near Kia’s plant. The site offers covered fast charging, 400 kW hardware, both NACS and CCS connectors, and on-site basics like restrooms and vending, which is much closer to the convenience drivers expect from a normal roadside stop.

The company’s Beacon concept goes even further. Ionna says those flagship sites are designed with 20 or more ultra-fast bays, canopies over every stall, restrooms, interior lounge space, retail, outdoor seating, and lighting meant to make the stop feel safer and more comfortable.

The network is expanding in several ways.

Ionna is not building every site in exactly the same format. Its network now includes full Rechargery hubs, lighter Rechargery Relay stops, and co-branded Rechargery at partner locations, which gives the company more flexibility as it expands.

That strategy also helps explain the partnerships with familiar roadside names. Ionna has already announced deals with Sheetz and Wawa, using existing convenience and fuel locations to speed up growth while keeping the kind of amenities drivers already know how to use.

The scale of the rollout is getting harder to ignore. Ionna said in March 2026 that it had nearly 1,000 live bays across the country, while earlier company updates pointed to more than 3,000 contracted bays and a longer-term target of 30,000 by 2030.

Big Automakers Are Betting On Better Infrastructure

This was never a small standalone startup story. Ionna was created by BMW, General Motors, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, and Stellantis, with Toyota joining later, which gives the project unusual backing for a charging network still in its early years.

The timing is important because the EV market has grown more complicated. Federal clean vehicle credits ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and Reuters reported that automakers have already adjusted product plans in response to that tougher environment.

That is why Ionna’s mission may matter beyond the chargers themselves. If EVs are entering a more demanding second phase, one shaped less by novelty and more by everyday practicality, then the quality of the charging stop may end up influencing adoption almost as much as the vehicles parked there.

title: Years of drought has major energy port of Corpus Christi, Texas, wrestling with water crisis
description:
Experts said the city didn’t expect such a bad drought, and new sources of reliable water didn’t arrive as expected.
Corpus Christi, a city of about 317,000 people that also supplies water to nearby counties, is closely tied to its oil and gas industry.
City officials had allowed for drought in their calculations — just not this kind of drought, Zanoni said.
Companies have stopped landscaping, they recycle water for essential cooling needs and they are looking for alternative water sources, he said.
The city is in a water emergency when it has 180 days before water supply can’t keep up with demand.
text:
In parched southern Texas, a yearslong drought has depleted Corpus Christi’s water reserves so gravely that the city is scrambling to prevent a shortage that could force painful cutbacks for residents and hobble the refineries and petrochemical plants in a major energy port.

Experts said the city didn’t expect such a bad drought, and new sources of reliable water didn’t arrive as expected. Those problems arose as the city increased its water sales to big industrial customers.

“We just have not kept up with water supply and water infrastructure like we should have. And it’s decades in the making,” said Peter Zanoni, the city manager since 2019.

Corpus Christi, a city of about 317,000 people that also supplies water to nearby counties, is closely tied to its oil and gas industry. The region makes everyday essentials like fuel and steel and ships them to the world.

Zanoni said it is highly unlikely the city will run out of water, but without significant rainfall or new sources, residents may face forced cutbacks and industry may have to do with less. At a time when the Iran war is already raising gas prices, the shortage is hitting an area that produces 5% of the U.S. gasoline supply.

Droughts are common, but this one has dragged on for most of the past seven years. Key reservoirs are at their lowest point ever. The quickest fix is different weather.

“We are actively praying for a hurricane,” former city council member David Loeb said, half in jest. Loeb doesn’t want anyone injured, but after wrestling with previous droughts in his time on the council, he feels the lack of rain acutely.

The drought isn’t expected to lift by summer, leaving officials scrambling to tap more groundwater to avoid an emergency.

Lessons from last time

After the last drought in the early 2010s, the city approved a pipeline extension to bring in more water from the Colorado River and promoted conservation. In the years that followed, water use actually fell. The city, seeing opportunity, added a petrochemical plant and steel mill to its long list of industrial customers.

City officials had allowed for drought in their calculations — just not this kind of drought, Zanoni said. It has hit especially hard because reservoirs never fully recharged after the last one.

And it’s come at a bad time.

After many years, the pipeline extension finally delivered its full capacity only last year. Meanwhile, discussion of building a desalination plant that would remove salt from seawater — a potentially drought-proof solution recommended in 2016 — bogged down over concerns about costs as high as $1.3 billion and environmental impact.

“If the then-city council had followed through on that, we would have had that plant up and running by now,” Zanoni said.

It’s an industry town

Corpus Christi has followed its long-established plan for reducing water use. Stage 1 seeks voluntary actions from citizens like taking shorter showers and limiting how often they can water. Currently, the city is in Stage 3, which means pauses on many outdoor water uses.

Many residents are angry that they can’t water their lawns, that their bills are set to rise sharply and that they may face fines, said Isabel Araiza, co-founder of a grassroots group active on water issues. Some don’t feel industry will be asked to share in the pain, she said.

The city’s drought plan allows for charging residents and businesses extra if they use lots of water. But big industry, which Zanoni says consumes as much as 60% of the city’s water, can opt to pay a permanent surcharge to avoid the possibility of having a much larger fee added in times of drought.

Araiza calls it a bad system. Once industry pays the surcharge, she said, they have no incentive to conserve water.

The city has defended the system, saying in a statement that industry does not “get a pass on water conservation” or forced curtailment. The statement said the business surcharges have raised $6 million a year.

It is wrong to suggest industry isn’t helping, said Bob Paulison, executive director of the Coastal Bend Industry Association. Companies have stopped landscaping, they recycle water for essential cooling needs and they are looking for alternative water sources, he said.

The city hasn’t imposed extra costs on anyone yet.

But Zanoni said water rates may eventually double as the city invests roughly $1 billion on infrastructure — costs that some argue will disproportionately benefit industry and make life for residents more expensive.

What’s the way out?

The city is in a water emergency when it has 180 days before water supply can’t keep up with demand. Officials have run through different scenarios for getting new water and the drought easing, and have said an emergency could come as early as May, as late as October, or not at all.

The city has tapped into millions of gallons of new groundwater, and it hopes to get even more.

The biggest unknown is the Evangeline Groundwater Project, which involves a pipeline and about two dozen wells that could add enough water to head off an emergency. It still needs state approval but the city hopes water could be flowing as soon as November. New sources come with drawbacks – some have raised water quality concerns, and there are worries too much pumping could deplete groundwater.

If the city has to declare a water emergency, it would be able to more aggressively curtail water use – mandatory reductions that would apply evenly to all industry and residents. That is a sensitive decision and is likely to be a “knock-down drag-out bloodbath,” Loeb said.

Because residents on average have already reduced their water use, future mandatory cuts are likely to fall heavier on industry.

“It’ll be an unbelievable disaster,” said Don Roach, former assistant general manager of the San Patricio Municipal Water District that has lots of industrial customers in the area. “When you cut the cooling water off to most of these industries, they just have to shut down. There’s no other way around it.”

Paulison said companies that produce fuel, polymers, iron and steel “have the least amount of flexibility in just cutting water usage.” He added, however, that companies remain optimistic they can reduce usage, adapt and continue operations.

Zanoni said the city’s plans should buy time to avert the worst.

“We are hoping we don’t get there, but we don’t work on hope,” he said.

text:
Archbald is a little corner of northeastern Pennsylvania where coal used to be big business. But now, there is a new boom: data centers.

Kayleigh Cornell, a teacher, and Sarah Gabriel, an ICU nurse, run a neighborhood association in this community of 7,000, where a half-dozen data centers have been proposed. "It is a really nice small town," said Gabriel. "It feels like home."

Cornell said, "I just really love it, and I can't imagine being anywhere else."

But they, and others, are alarmed about the possible impact of data centers on the environment, their electric bills, and the town's character.

Gabriel said, "It's gonna just completely change the landscape. Anywhere there's trees, there's probably not going to be any any longer."

Cornell says they are determined: "We'll stop it if we could help it."

Stopping it won't be easy. Demand is huge: tech companies say they need these massive structures, full of computing power, to fuel the AI revolution. So, developers are rushing to build them in places like Archbald – rich in land, water and power. But there is an intensifying debate over the scope of jobs and revenue they bring. And many communities are on edge over rising electric utility bills.

In Archbald, the push to slow things down has upended local politics. At a March 10 borough meeting, where many held up signs reading "No data centers," residents yelled at representatives of the proposed centers to "get out of here."

"We made up our minds: go home!" One woman shouted.

One project, an application for a campus of 18 data centers, has hit a roadblock.

Data center concerns prompt regime change in Archbald (WVIA)

Sarah Gabriel says fighting AI superpowers wasn't part of her plan: "We're not against AI data centers. But because the industry is so new and unregulated, it is concerning that if we just keep moving forward, we're gonna get to, like, a point of no return."

Elsewhere, data centers are already a way of life, with more than 4,000 (and counting) in operation across the country, and many more going up around the world.

In Loudoun County, Virginia, known as "Data Center Alley," anonymous, sci-fi-looking buildings seem to be everywhere. One is slightly more than one-million square feet – big enough to park two aircraft carriers.

Andy Power, president and CEO of Digital Realty, which owns and operates hundreds of data centers globally, says the data center sector is valued at hundreds of billions of dollars, and represents "the breakthroughs that cure new diseases, that'll, say, essentially improve quality of life."

Asked to respond to those who don't want data centers in their communities, Power replied, "I would say, 'I completely understand it. Let me tell you why this location makes the most sense for the data centers. And this infrastructure's gonna help change the world you're living in today and for years to come.'"

In Washington, there are fierce critics calling for a moratorium on data center construction until tougher AI regulations are enacted by Congress. Last month, Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, an Independent, and New York Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Data Center Moratorium Act.

"I fear that Congress is totally unprepared for the magnitude of the changes that are already taking place," Sanders said.

But President Trump and many Republicans say data centers are vital for our future economy.

Senator Dave McCormick, a Pennsylvania Republican, has worked to bring data-center investments to his home state. He calls American leadership in AI "the most important question facing our country.

"I think the net benefit for Pennsylvania is enormous," he said.

McCormick adds that data centers need to work with – not against – communities, but wants companies building in his state. "There's got to be a covenant," he said. "There's got to be a promise that goes from the community to those that are developing in the community of what kind of job creation; how they're going to protect the environment; how they're going to protect water supply; how they're going to protect energy costs. When a community looks at the totality of the jobs, the tax revenue, the new roads, the libraries, the schools, the opportunity of jobs for their kids, I think these are pretty compelling."

Back in Archbald, the data centers continue to move forward, and for Kayleigh Cornell and Sarah Gabriel, it's a reality they're grappling with every day

"People live here 'cause of the quality of life," Cornell said. "Yes, obviously you need jobs. But, again, this would be intrinsically changing the character of Archbald Borough."

Asked if they feel they have a fighting chance to stop it, Gabriel replied, "Yeah, absolutely."

"We have no other alternative," Cornell said. "I mean, it's our home. We have to fight."

Slate Auto Emerges: A Disruptive Force in Electric Vehicles

April 2025 marked the public debut of Slate Auto, a startup that had been quietly developing an affordable, highly customizable electric pickup truck in Troy, Michigan for three years. Backed by Jeff Bezos, Slate Auto surprised the automotive world, operating in close proximity to industry giants like Ford and General Motors.

TechCrunch broke the news in early April, uncovering Slate Auto’s secret operations, its connection to the Amazon founder, and its unconventional business approach. In the weeks following the initial report, prototypes of Slate’s truck began appearing throughout California, generating significant buzz ahead of the company’s official launch.

Slate Auto: A Unique Player in the EV Landscape

While many U.S. EV startups have struggled with bankruptcies and failed launches, Slate Auto stands out with its innovative team, strong financial backing, and distinctive business model. Despite these advantages, the company faces numerous challenges as it aims to begin production by late 2026.

Below is a comprehensive timeline highlighting the key milestones in Slate Auto’s journey, from its inception and investors to its product development and manufacturing plans.

Jeff Bezos’ Secret Investment in Slate Auto

April 8 – After a year of investigation, TechCrunch revealed that Slate Auto had been operating covertly for three years, supported financially by Jeff Bezos and Mark Walter, owner of the LA Dodgers.

Slate Auto differentiated itself by focusing on a budget-friendly electric pickup truck, targeting a starting price of $25,000. The vehicle’s customization options drew on the expertise of former Harley-Davidson and Chrysler employees, known for their work in accessories and aftermarket parts.

First Public Sighting of Slate’s Electric Truck

April 10 – A photo of an unidentified electric truck surfaced on the subreddit, sparking speculation that it was Slate’s new EV. TechCrunch later confirmed the vehicle was indeed a prototype parked outside Slate’s design center in Long Beach, California.

Modular EVs: Slate’s “Transformer” Concept

April 21 – Slate began showcasing concept vehicles on public roads to build anticipation ahead of its launch event. Some of these prototypes resembled SUVs or hatchbacks, highlighting the brand’s commitment to modular, “Transformer-like” customization capabilities. This demonstration was intended to tease the flexibility of their upcoming EV.

Slate’s Anti-Tesla Approach: The Analog Pickup Truck

April 24 – At its launch event in Long Beach, Slate Auto introduced its customizable electric pickup truck, announcing a price below $20,000 when factoring in the $7,500 federal EV tax credit. The base model featured minimal amenities: 150 miles of range, no power windows, no infotainment screen, and no paint. Buyers could personalize nearly every aspect, from seating to the vehicle’s shape.

Manufacturing Plans: Indiana Printing Plant Selected

April 25 – TechCrunch reported that Slate Auto had chosen a former printing facility in Warsaw, Indiana as its manufacturing site. The 1.4 million-square-foot plant, built in 1958, had been unused for about two years and would serve as the company’s factory.

Reservation Milestones: Over 100,000 in Two Weeks

May 12 – Slate Auto announced it had received more than 100,000 refundable $50 reservations for its affordable EV truck, demonstrating widespread interest despite the company’s recent emergence.

Pricing Changes After Federal Tax Credit Ends

July 3 – Following the Trump administration’s tax-cut bill, which ended the $7,500 federal EV tax credit in September, Slate Auto removed its “under $20,000” pricing claim from its website, as the credit was no longer available to buyers.

Early Investment: LA-Based VC Firm’s Involvement

July 8 – Slate’s 2023 funding round attracted at least 16 investors, including Jeff Bezos. Los Angeles-based Slauson & Co. discussed with TechCrunch their decision to invest early in Slate Auto, participating in both the initial round and Series B.

Slate Auto Takes the Stage at TechCrunch Disrupt

October 30 – CEO Chris Barman appeared at TechCrunch Disrupt 2025, sharing insights about Jeff Bezos’ involvement, the challenges of launching a new automaker, and plans to create a marketplace for vehicle customization.

Growing Demand: 150,000 Reservations Reached

December 16 – Despite a slowdown in EV adoption across the U.S., Slate Auto surpassed 150,000 refundable reservations for its truck and SUV. This milestone indicated strong consumer interest, even after the federal tax credit was discontinued. With fewer competitors in the affordable EV segment, Slate Auto is poised to capture a significant share of the market.

2026: Leadership Changes and Launch Preparations

text:
The decision to build America's first new refinery in over 50 years represents a significant moment for domestic energy infrastructure.

As Fluor Corporation takes on the engineering and design of this large-scale facility in Texas, the project highlights growing concerns about supply chain vulnerabilities and the need for more resilient logistics networks in the oil sector.

The US has experienced significant imbalances in its oil supply chain operations. Between 2014 and 2024, the country imported 28 billion barrels of crude oil while exporting nearly 10 billion barrels overseas.

This gap illustrates the complex logistics challenges and supply chain dependencies that have made America vulnerable to global disruptions. When oil supply chains face interruptions, the impacts ripple across industries, leading to price volatility and resource scarcity that can bring operations to a standstill.

Sustainability, procurement and supply chain leaders won’t want to miss Procurement & Supply Chain LIVE, taking place at Navy Pier, Chicago, on April 21–22.

Co-located with Sustainability LIVE: The US Summit, the event unites senior decision-makers at a time when supply chains, sustainability and business performance are more interdependent than ever.

Secure your place now for The US Summit – group booking discounts available.

Strengthening domestic infrastructure

America First Refining (AFR) is addressing these supply chain weaknesses by developing a hydrogen-powered refinery in Brownsville, Texas. The facility aims to redirect up to 60m barrels annually from international supply routes to domestic processing channels, potentially reducing logistics complexity and transportation costs associated with imported crude oil.

The project, currently in Phase I of construction, has selected Fluor Corporation to engineer and design the facility. According to AFR, the refinery will utilise commercially proven technologies from leading American and global engineering firms to produce high-octane, cleaner fuels.

The facility will process American shale oil into gasoline, jet fuel and diesel, creating a more direct supply chain from domestic extraction to refined products.

The use of excess produced hydrogen could enable the production of low-emission fuels, potentially positioning the facility as infrastructure that addresses both supply chain resilience and environmental considerations. However, the full logistics implications of hydrogen integration remain to be seen as the project develops.

Logistics advantages and positioning

The facility's location within the Port of Brownsville offers significant supply chain benefits. This deep-water port, spanning 40,000 acres, is the largest land-owning public port authority in the US and serves as a key hub for energy, shipbuilding and ship recycling. The port's existing infrastructure for handling natural gas liquids, bulk petroleum, refined products and other specialised bulk liquids could provide efficient distribution networks for the refinery's output.

Situating the complex within a foreign trade zone adds another logistics dimension, potentially offering supply chain advantages related to customs procedures and inventory management. The port's role as a transportation and industrial growth hub suggests the refinery will benefit from established logistics networks and infrastructure that can support both inbound crude oil deliveries and outbound refined product distribution.

Fluor Corporation brings relevant experience to the infrastructure challenges. The American engineering and construction company provides services across oil & gas, industrial & infrastructure and government & power sectors. With headquarters in Texas and more than 50 years of experience in engineering, procurement, construction and maintenance services, Fluor will execute the front-end engineering and design for the facility.

"We are honoured to partner with America First Refining on this landmark US project," says Pierre Bechelany, Fluor's Business Group President of Energy Solutions.

"Together, AFR and Fluor bring deep technical expertise and proven project‑delivery capabilities, positioning the project for successful execution. This collaboration reflects both companies' commitment to advancing the nation's refining infrastructure."

The contract value remains undisclosed, though Fluor is set to recognise it in the first quarter of 2026. Following completion, the facility is estimated to process more than 60 million barrels of domestic crude oil annually, which could represent a significant shift in domestic supply chain flows and reduce dependence on international logistics networks that have proven vulnerable to disruption.

This infrastructure development reflects broader efforts to build more resilient domestic supply chains across industries. By establishing processing capacity closer to extraction points and major distribution hubs, the project could reduce transportation distances, simplify logistics coordination and create redundancy in refining capacity that might prove valuable during future supply chain disruptions.

title: Guest Post: Age Matters - A Business Student Learns About Energy Efficiency
description:

text:
This article was published in Scientific American’s former blog network and reflects the views of the author, not necessarily those of Scientific American

By Kelsey Morris

As a summer intern at Go Green Squads, I worked on projects related to increasing the energy efficiency of residential buildings in Austin. Over a summer full of record high temperatures, including more than 80 days above 100 degrees, I saw first-hand how energy efficiency could potentially impact entire communities. I also learned how a business student could contribute to a field that I had previously thought was purely technical.

Before this summer I had a vague notion of what the term “energy efficiency” meant and had concluded that it was one of those complex problems that engineers dealt with. Efficiency meant improved lightbulbs and appliances. But, this summer, as temperatures rose and stayed high in my community in Austin, I was able to learn about ways to successfully apply my business background in this field.

On supporting science journalism

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

This summer I interned for a start-up company that performs energy audits and upgrades for houses and apartment complexes in the Austin area. Energy audits give homeowners information about energy usage in their homes, which cannot be seen on a monthly energy bill. In addition, energy upgrades such as weatherization can offer these residents cost effective solutions that provide valuable saving to residents by reducing the amount of energy needed in the home. As a business intern at Go Green Squads, I had the job of putting together quotes for energy efficiency improvements and was able to learn first-hand the expense of improving the efficiency of individual homes, and the energy cost if these upgrades are not made.

As a business student, I have taken classes on statistical modeling and accounting. In these classes, I learned the basics of regression equations, price modeling, and costing principles, which gave me the foundation necessary to prepare price estimates for potential customers who wanted to see if “energy efficiency” was in their budget. In the process of preparing these quotes, I found that assumptions I had made regarding what would impact the cost were generally not correct. And, I was able to help improve the efficiency of the energy auditing process.

Initially, I believed that the square footage and age of a home would be the best indicators of the price of infiltration work – improving the efficiency of the home’s building work - for a residential house. But, after seeing the results of many blower door tests and insulation evaluations, I found that this relationship didn’t appear to be completely correct. In order to confirm my suspicion, I conducted some base-level statistical analysis on the data that we gathered during our energy audits. After processing these data, I found that just the age of the home could be used to provide a reasonable price estimate for the infiltration work on that home.

What does that mean for homeowners looking to do efficiency upgrades in the Austin area? If you own an older home you may need more infiltration work, and should consider focusing your energy upgrades in that area. If you have a newer house that will likely need less infiltration work, you may want to consider additional efficiency upgrades for your home. Further, when targeting areas for energy efficiency improvements, the average age of homes in the area could be used as the primary factor in identifying areas that might need significant upgrades.

What did this analysis mean for me? It showed me how a business student could contribute to improving the energy efficiency of our buildings. And, in turn, this experience showed me how a business background can help reduce our energy demand. While we don’t all have the training to build a wind farm or a power plant, we do have individual skills that can help our communities to become more efficient.

About the Author:

Kelsey Morris is a third year business student at the University of Texas at Austin and will graduate with a degree in Energy Finance in May 2013. In addition to working toward her Bachelors in Business Administration (BBA) in Finance, Kelsey is participating in the Bridging Disciplines Program, an academic program that allows university students to take cross-disciplinary coursework on a particular subject. Within this program Kelsey is studying social entrepreneurship and nonprofits with an environmental focus.

Currently, Kelsey serves as Vice President of the University of Texas chapter of Net Impact Undergraduate. Net Impact Undergraduate (NIU) focuses on educating students about sustainability and connecting students with socially responsible professionals and businesses. In the spring of 2012, Kelsey will study abroad at the University of Economics in Prague, Czech Republic. Kelsey can be contacted via e-mail at kelsey.morris @ bba09.mccombs.utexas.edu.

title: Years of drought has major energy port of Corpus Christi, Texas, wrestling with water crisis
description:
Experts said the city didn’t expect such a bad drought, and new sources of reliable water didn’t arrive as expected.
Corpus Christi, a city of about 317,000 people that also supplies water to nearby counties, is closely tied to its oil and gas industry.
City officials had allowed for drought in their calculations — just not this kind of drought, Zanoni said.
Companies have stopped landscaping, they recycle water for essential cooling needs and they are looking for alternative water sources, he said.
The city is in a water emergency when it has 180 days before water supply can’t keep up with demand.
text:
In parched southern Texas, a yearslong drought has depleted Corpus Christi’s water reserves so gravely that the city is scrambling to prevent a shortage that could force painful cutbacks for residents and hobble the refineries and petrochemical plants in a major energy port.

Experts said the city didn’t expect such a bad drought, and new sources of reliable water didn’t arrive as expected. Those problems arose as the city increased its water sales to big industrial customers.

“We just have not kept up with water supply and water infrastructure like we should have. And it’s decades in the making,” said Peter Zanoni, the city manager since 2019.

Corpus Christi, a city of about 317,000 people that also supplies water to nearby counties, is closely tied to its oil and gas industry. The region makes everyday essentials like fuel and steel and ships them to the world.

Zanoni said it is highly unlikely the city will run out of water, but without significant rainfall or new sources, residents may face forced cutbacks and industry may have to do with less. At a time when the Iran war is already raising gas prices, the shortage is hitting an area that produces 5% of the U.S. gasoline supply.

Droughts are common, but this one has dragged on for most of the past seven years. Key reservoirs are at their lowest point ever. The quickest fix is different weather.

“We are actively praying for a hurricane,” former city council member David Loeb said, half in jest. Loeb doesn’t want anyone injured, but after wrestling with previous droughts in his time on the council, he feels the lack of rain acutely.

The drought isn’t expected to lift by summer, leaving officials scrambling to tap more groundwater to avoid an emergency.

Lessons from last time

After the last drought in the early 2010s, the city approved a pipeline extension to bring in more water from the Colorado River and promoted conservation. In the years that followed, water use actually fell. The city, seeing opportunity, added a petrochemical plant and steel mill to its long list of industrial customers.

City officials had allowed for drought in their calculations — just not this kind of drought, Zanoni said. It has hit especially hard because reservoirs never fully recharged after the last one.

And it’s come at a bad time.

After many years, the pipeline extension finally delivered its full capacity only last year. Meanwhile, discussion of building a desalination plant that would remove salt from seawater — a potentially drought-proof solution recommended in 2016 — bogged down over concerns about costs as high as $1.3 billion and environmental impact.

“If the then-city council had followed through on that, we would have had that plant up and running by now,” Zanoni said.

It’s an industry town

Corpus Christi has followed its long-established plan for reducing water use. Stage 1 seeks voluntary actions from citizens like taking shorter showers and limiting how often they can water. Currently, the city is in Stage 3, which means pauses on many outdoor water uses.

Many residents are angry that they can’t water their lawns, that their bills are set to rise sharply and that they may face fines, said Isabel Araiza, co-founder of a grassroots group active on water issues. Some don’t feel industry will be asked to share in the pain, she said.

The city’s drought plan allows for charging residents and businesses extra if they use lots of water. But big industry, which Zanoni says consumes as much as 60% of the city’s water, can opt to pay a permanent surcharge to avoid the possibility of having a much larger fee added in times of drought.

Araiza calls it a bad system. Once industry pays the surcharge, she said, they have no incentive to conserve water.

The city has defended the system, saying in a statement that industry does not “get a pass on water conservation” or forced curtailment. The statement said the business surcharges have raised $6 million a year.

It is wrong to suggest industry isn’t helping, said Bob Paulison, executive director of the Coastal Bend Industry Association. Companies have stopped landscaping, they recycle water for essential cooling needs and they are looking for alternative water sources, he said.

The city hasn’t imposed extra costs on anyone yet.

But Zanoni said water rates may eventually double as the city invests roughly $1 billion on infrastructure — costs that some argue will disproportionately benefit industry and make life for residents more expensive.

What’s the way out?

The city is in a water emergency when it has 180 days before water supply can’t keep up with demand. Officials have run through different scenarios for getting new water and the drought easing, and have said an emergency could come as early as May, as late as October, or not at all.

The city has tapped into millions of gallons of new groundwater, and it hopes to get even more.

The biggest unknown is the Evangeline Groundwater Project, which involves a pipeline and about two dozen wells that could add enough water to head off an emergency. It still needs state approval but the city hopes water could be flowing as soon as November. New sources come with drawbacks – some have raised water quality concerns, and there are worries too much pumping could deplete groundwater.

If the city has to declare a water emergency, it would be able to more aggressively curtail water use – mandatory reductions that would apply evenly to all industry and residents. That is a sensitive decision and is likely to be a “knock-down drag-out bloodbath,” Loeb said.

Because residents on average have already reduced their water use, future mandatory cuts are likely to fall heavier on industry.

“It’ll be an unbelievable disaster,” said Don Roach, former assistant general manager of the San Patricio Municipal Water District that has lots of industrial customers in the area. “When you cut the cooling water off to most of these industries, they just have to shut down. There’s no other way around it.”

Paulison said companies that produce fuel, polymers, iron and steel “have the least amount of flexibility in just cutting water usage.” He added, however, that companies remain optimistic they can reduce usage, adapt and continue operations.

Zanoni said the city’s plans should buy time to avert the worst.

“We are hoping we don’t get there, but we don’t work on hope,” he said.
